title: Critique of Pagan Mythology
english: The critique of pagan mythology is not limited to the Jews, but extends to all nations, for Galilee is a part of the nations, and it is unclear and not yet clear against whom the word would be more appropriately and truthfully directed.
This uncertainty raises questions about whether the critique should be directed against the Christians or against those who have honored the unblameable and dear superstition.
The Galileans themselves would not be suspected of harmonizing with the Greek thunderbolts, which are often used to describe the power of pagan mythology.

The poets have made the most of a madness that is not inspired by God, but is from elsewhere, resulting in the greatest outcry, and it is fitting to speak openly about the foolishness of their chatter.

For example, Plato does not accept the gods and goddesses of Homer, who have been condemned for their shamelessness and injustices against humans, and who weep and mourn for their dead relatives, and speak in a womanly manner, because they want to escape death but are unable to do so, and are defeated by the Fates and yield to what is destined, as if they were weaker than the leader of the other gods, whom they call Zeus.
However, the ability to say many things is not necessarily a benefit, and it is more important to focus on the goal of understanding the truth.

The Greeks are known for their mythological stories, and they have used these tales to create a false sense of reality, leading people away from the truth, and by inventing monstrous fabrications, they have imposed a wicked fabrication against the unspeakable glory of the God who rules all, and they have set up a snare for the simpler souls.

As the all-wise Paul writes, 'they have become foolish, saying they are wise, and they have exchanged the glory of the immortal God for the likeness of a mortal man and birds and four-footed animals and reptiles' (Romans 1:23).

We must yield to the thoughts of the holy apostles and allow them to examine the things said, so that they may show clearly what the wickedly fabricated fabrication is, what kind of monstrous fabrication it is, and what the love of myth and childishness of the Christian religion is.

Moses wrote to us about the one true God, describing Him as ungenerated, eternal, incorruptible, without quantity, invisible, unchangeable, without beginning, life and life-giving, wisdom, power, creator, king, Lord of all, and it is unlikely that the word of the holy prophets would deviate from these Mosaic doctrines, or that the teaching of the apostles would be different.

On the contrary, it is not at all plausible that the things taught by the Galileans would lack a divine element, being instead mere myths and fictions, for who would not agree that there is nothing better for humans than to have a clear and accurate understanding of the one creator and Lord of all, who exists by nature and truly?

This understanding is the most beautiful and exceptional part of philosophy, and it is through the theoretical aspect of philosophy that those who are able to see can gain a deeper understanding of God, and since our opponent claims to be persuaded of his views, let him explain from where or from whom he derived his knowledge, and demonstrate the validity of his claims, rather than merely boasting about his knowledge.

When considering the arguments of those who accuse, it is essential to examine their validity and truthfulness, and the accuser should not merely persuade himself, but rather provide proof through his actions, and in doing so, he will ultimately be writing against himself in judgment, rather than against us, regarding the fabrication of which he speaks.

Furthermore, when engaging in a discussion about the doctrines in question, it is crucial to establish a clear and orderly approach, avoiding external distractions and counter-accusations, until the initial points have been adequately addressed, and it is preferable to establish a clear and distinct line of argumentation when addressing accusations, and to refrain from counter-accusations when responding to criticisms.

Moreover, if one were to accuse the Christian religion and yet fail to acknowledge its worth, instead opting to extol the superstition of the Greeks with the highest honors, then it is only fitting that they should demand the same level of recognition in return, but if they boast with their words and try to elevate their own reputation by disparaging ours, using poor counsel, they set the Greeks up as superior, implying that we should remain silent and not respond to their criticisms.

However, if we were to focus solely on recalling the teachings of the Greeks, it would seem that their discussion is reasonable and not unlikely, but when they want to engage with us and respond to every point we make, how can they justly criticize us for exposing the shame of Greek impiety and their own foolishness?

The fact is, just as colors are more visible when set against a different background, the inherent beauties of virtues become more apparent to ignorant minds when seen in contrast to the ugliness of their opposites, and the shame of wickedness makes the necessity of conquering more apparent to those who are better.

Therefore, it is likely that our critics fear their own teachings and do not want them to be examined, which is why they command us to be silent and accuse us in other ways as well, and to understand the roots of our ideas, it is essential to consider the concept of God and how it was formed.

We must examine what the Greeks and Hebrews have said about the divine, and then look at those who are neither Greeks nor Jews, but rather from Galilee, who have chosen some things from these sources before our time, but they do not even follow these things, and have abandoned them to create their own path, which they claim is the best kind of piety, taking atheism from Jewish recklessness and a base and servile life from Greek laziness and cowardice, to create a unique and misguided form of worship.

translator_notes: The Greek text contains the phrase 'καταβοήν' which is translated as 'the outcry' or 'the lament'.

The phrase 'πρέπει δὲ ὅτι τῆς παρ' αὐτοῖς τερθρείας ἀποφοιτᾶν ἀναφανδὸν εἰπεῖν' is translated as 'it is fitting that the power of what is said about them should be brought to bear, and it seems that the shame of their foolishness should be exposed'.

title: Critique of Greek Philosophy
english: It does not seem that someone who abandons confession and the need to slander himself will be upright before the judges he will meet, as if he wanted to learn from them what is better or worse.
However, this will not happen among those who know the power of truth and the weakness of falsehood.
Perhaps he thinks that some will praise his opinion about God if he does not criticize the Christians by comparing them unfavorably to the Greeks, who accept the shameful vote against themselves.
When we make arguments about our own religion, we should be silent and remember our own teachings, which he himself has rejected.
Since they introduce and believe the myths, we might ask why we, leaving the Greeks, turn to the Hebrews.

Let us tell him that since you have left the Christians and run away from the truth, loving falsehood, and preferring the most foolish worship of idolaters to the accurate glory of God, you do not counsel well, but rather will suffer the worst reputation.

The Greek myths are filled with absurd and unbelievable stories, such as the one where Zeus mixed with his mother, became a father from her, married his own daughter, or rather did not marry his own daughter but having mixed with another he handed her over, and then there are the stories of Dionysus being torn apart and his limbs being put back together again.
For Moses, the prophets, apostles, and evangelists all glorify the one true God and teach us to live in a noble manner, rejecting the shameful and unbelievable myths of the Greeks.
The power of their teaching is in harmony with the concepts of the Old Testament, and this will become clear to us in due time (Genesis 1:1).
Let him demonstrate that nothing good or noble exists among us, and let the accusation not be without basis.
For we possess a profound understanding of the most serious matters, and among Christians, the discourse about God and the creation of the world is characterized by accuracy and purity.
Our knowledge of practices, derived from the holy Scriptures, is blameless and unassailable (Matthew 5:48).
It is evident that the best philosophy would be achieved through this approach, which encompasses both theoretical and practical aspects, and is admired by those who have studied Greek philosophy.

We have not learned atheism from the Hebrews, but rather, through the God-inspired Scripture, we have come to recognize the ignorance of the Greeks, and the concept of atheism is more prevalent among those who do not know God by nature and truth (Psalm 14:1).

They choose a bad and indulgent life because of their laziness, criticizing our supposed gluttony and laziness, calling it a Greek trait, and saying we eat without distinction and do not abstain from any foods.
What kind of purity do they define in these matters, when everything has been made by God, and all things from the good are good?
The all-pure and blameless one would not do anything to defile us (1 John 3:3).
The act of eating and drinking would not bring any benefit to those who partake of it, nor would it introduce any kind of defilement.
It is only fitting to abstain from things that could potentially defile one, such as the ways of wickedness, including adultery, fornication, slander, and love of money (Galatians 5:19-21).
Some individuals, however, pretend to be ascetics, sometimes even abstaining from certain foods, but they show no fear of outward things.
Instead, they flatter the ruler and serve the power of the Cyprian goddess.
The book of creation says nothing true, but rather heaps up nonsense, and what was worthy of consideration, it does everything without reason.
It strongly rejects the all-wise Moses and his writings, making a great denial.
I am amazed at the opinions of the Greek wise men, especially the praises and applause of Plato.
I will try to speak about the probability of their discoveries.
It is necessary to set forth again the opinions of the philosophers regarding the construction of the world, which they thought worthy of consideration.
Then, we will present the cosmogony of Moses.
By doing so, it will become clear to those who encounter it that the discourse of the philosophers is lacking, while the writings of Moses are characterized by clarity and truth.
Plutarch, a notable figure among the philosophers, discusses the world in the second book of his collection of physical doctrines.
He notes that Pythagoras was the first to use the term 'cosmos' to describe the ordered universe.
Thales and his followers believed in a single world.
In contrast, Democritus, Epicurus, and his teacher Metrodorus proposed the existence of infinite worlds in an infinite universe, with each world having its own unique characteristics.
Empedocles believed that the orbit of the sun marked the boundary of the world.
Seleucus argued that the world is infinite.
Diogenes took a different view, suggesting that the whole universe is infinite, but the world itself is limited.
The Stoics, meanwhile, distinguished between the whole universe and the world, arguing that the whole includes the infinite void, while the world does not.
According to them, the whole and the world are ultimately the same.
Epicurus believed that the worlds could be spherical in shape, but also possibly have other forms.
When considering whether the world is animate or not, the philosophers were divided.
Most argued that it is indeed animate and governed by providence.

However, Democritus and Epicurus, along with those who propose the existence of atoms and the void, suggest that the world is neither animate nor governed by providence, but rather by some irrational natural force.
Aristotle does not consider the world as a whole to be animate, logical, intellectual, or governed by providence.
According to Aristotle, the heavenly bodies share in all these qualities.
The spheres contain animate and living things, whereas the earthly realm does not participate in any of these aspects.
The orderliness of the earthly realm is merely accidental.
The philosophers also have varying opinions on the nature of the world.
Some, like Pythagoras and the Stoics, believe it to be generated by God and perishable by nature.
Others, like Epicurus, argue that it is perishable because it is generated, much like an animal or a plant.
Xenophanes posits that the world is ungenerated, eternal, and imperishable.
Aristotle himself believes that the part of the world under the moon is subject to change and corruption, which also affects the earthly realm.
translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences might be cut off, but the translation aims to preserve the original word order and meaning as much as possible.
The term 'discoveries' is used to translate the Greek term 'εὑρεσιεπείαις', which may have a more nuanced meaning in the original context.
The allusion to the 'Book of Creation' is not a direct quote, but rather a reference to the idea that the book says nothing true.
The translation attempts to render the available text as literally as possible, while also conveying the author's intended meaning in natural literary prose.

title: Against Julian
english: Listen and understand how much nonsense is in these things, for when philosophers oppose each other's opinions, they investigate this and that carelessly and without examination, according to each one's opinion.

As a result, how can they not be considered guessers rather than knowers of the truth, given that some say the world is one, others say it is many, and yet others say it is created, while others say it is indestructible and ungenerated?

Some believe that the world is governed by God's providence, while others see it as without providence and its orderly motion is due to automatism and chance, which is evident in their arguments being tossed about like a drunkard.

However, Plato and Pythagoras seem to have more moderate views on the nature of God and the world, having received their education and knowledge from the Egyptians, among whom Moses was highly esteemed for his wisdom and teachings.

Despite this, Plato is accused of holding contradictory opinions, and his student Aristotle is said to have opposed and contradicted him, as Porphyry notes that Plato believed the heavens were composed of the four elements, harmonized by the soul.

According to Plato, the universe remains mixed and is named according to the majority, and he etymologizes the name, saying that the heaven is called as if it is visible, so that someone might think of the heaven from what is seen.
In contrast, Aristotle says that the heaven is not composed, nor is it made of the four elements, but he thinks of a fifth body, separate from the four and completely unmixed.

Plato claims that the world is animate and a rational living being, and he attributes providence to it, whereas his student Aristotle does not think this way, saying that the whole is not animate, nor rational, nor governed by providence.

Furthermore, Plato says that the world is generated and perishable, while Aristotle says that it is not generated, but imperishable and ungenerated, and Plato also posits that there are three principles of the universe: God, matter, and form.

He explains that God is the creator, matter is the substrate, and form is the paradigm of each thing, but Aristotle disagrees, saying that there are only two principles: God and matter, and that the form is not a principle.

Additionally, Plato introduces the soul as a fourth principle, in addition to God, matter, and form, and he says that matter is ungenerated, but also generated, which contradicts his own findings regarding form, for in the thoughts of God, form exists and does not have its own existence, that is, it does not have its own being.

Given the contradictions and disagreements among philosophers, to whom will the seekers of truth turn to follow the blameless and unerring path, and which of the named ones will we free from the charge of false speaking?

How can those who have sinned so greatly against the truth be considered worthy, given that they not only contradict each other but also their own opinions, as Julian praises and approves of these things, and mocks the account of Moses?
Let us compare the accounts of creation given by Plato and Moses, in order to see whose is better and more worthy of God.
Moses writes that God created the heaven and the earth in the beginning (Genesis 1:1), and that the earth was without form and void, with darkness over the face of the deep (Genesis 1:2).
Then, God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light, which God saw to be good (Genesis 1:3).
God also said, 'Let there be a firmament in the middle of the water,' and God called the firmament heaven (Genesis 1:6-8).
Next, God said, 'Let the water under the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear' (Genesis 1:9), and so it was.
Moreover, God said, 'Let the earth produce vegetation and fruit trees' (Genesis 1:11).

God also said, 'Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light on the earth' (Genesis 1:14-15), and God put these lights in the firmament to rule the day and the night (Genesis 1:16-18).

Notably, the account does not mention the creation of the abyss, darkness, or water by God, but rather focuses on the creation of the physical world, with no mention of the creation or making of angels, suggesting that God, according to Moses, is the decorator of existing matter, rather than the creator of nothing incorporeal.

The power of the miracles performed in Egypt would serve as a clear proof of the multifaceted virtue that resided within Moses, for he was a servant to God's will, working to undo the misconceptions of the Egyptians and guide their minds towards the truth.

Moses, not speaking idle words, nor driven by ambition, but rather devising something necessary for the benefit of life, did not intend to discuss natural philosophy or the first principles, but instead aimed to guide people's minds to the doctrines of truth.

For they were misled, worshiping what seemed right to each, and ignoring the one true God, with some attributing divinity to the sky, others to the sun, and others to various natural elements and creatures, demonstrating their deep-seated ignorance of the true nature of God.

As the situation had developed to this point, and such a terrible sickness had been distributed to all on the earth, Moses was a helper and a guide for all the most beautiful teachings, showing that the creator of all things is clearly proclaimed by nature.

He demonstrated that the other things, which were also provided through him, exist for the sake of being and existing in general, and having passed over the weak myth-making, Moses proceeded to the necessary discussion, without considering it necessary to discuss the nature of water or how it came to be in the beginning, nor to measure the depths and the nature of the heaven, but rather to discuss the way…
translator_notes: The text begins mid-sentence: 'εται.', and ends mid-sentence: 'τὸν τρόπον', indicating that it is a fragment of a larger work.
The Bible references are based on the Septuagint version of the Bible.
